newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew puts robot arm to work.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew puts robot arm to work.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Discovery on Thursday set their sights on Comet Hale-Bopp for a third look at the receding celestial snowball.

Astronaut Steve Robinson set up a $600,000 ultraviolet telescope in a porthole on Discovery's lower deck, while mission commander Curt Brown and co-pilot Kent Rominger kept the shuttle pointed at the comet, 270 million miles away.
Astronomers were hoping to learn more about the gas and dust spewing from Hale-Bopp as it speeds away from the sun at 50,000 mph (80,500 kph).
The shuttle's orbital observations were being complemented by infrared views from a telescope aboard a high flying aircraft. The astronauts planned a fourth and final look at the comet on Friday.
Mission control told the shuttle crew about the return to earth of Mir cosmonauts Vasily Tsibliev and Alexander Laztukin within seconds of their capsule touching down in Kazakhstan.
"We're glad they're safely on the ground," Brown said.
Throughout the flight, the shuttle crew have been kept informed of developments aboard Mir, where NASA astronaut Michael Foale has being living since May.
A week after blasting off, Discovery's crew continued to work with 24 major experiments as they orbited 185 miles (296 km) above the planet.
A free-flying satellite released by Discovery last week continued its check-up of the earth's upper atmosphere. The German-built spacecraft will be retrieved by the shuttle on Saturday.

Meanwhile, flight controllers in Houston said they were considering an extra workout on Friday for a Japanese prototype space station robot arm after tests on Wednesday were cut short by computer and communication difficulties.
Discovery is due to land at Florida's Kennedy Space Center on Monday.
